[PAPER_0202, relevance_score=0.319] Did high JTC participants reach their decisions on the task so quickly because they were more persuaded by initial pieces of evidence, consistent with a hypersalience hypothesis, or were they instead willing to reach a decision at lower levels of confidence, as suggested by the low threshold hypothesis? We also examined the final confidence participants expressed at the time they reached a decision for each lake. This analysis provided evidence for both hypotheses.

Jumping to Conclusions. First, participants will complete a task to assess their level of the jumping to conclusions (JTC) cognitive style. Participants will be confronted with a scenario in which they will observe a character fishing from one of two lakes. One lake will contain an 80% majority of red fish, with the rest being grey. The other will contain an 80% majority of grey fish, with the remaining minority being red.

[PREREG_0017, relevance_score=0.255] After completing this task, participants will repeat it with a new character and pair of lakes, in which the two lakes contained either a 65% majority of red or grey fish. The same rules applied as above.

 To measure a person's level of JTC bias, we will sum the number of fish they asked to see across the two lakes. We anticipate this variable will be skewed. Thus, to reduce skew, we will take the natural log of this number. We will reverse code this variable so that high jumpers means collected less information.

[PAPER_0056, relevance_score=0.237] We also conducted other analyses aimed at specifying the ingredient within JTC behavior that disrupts the quality of judgments. We tested whether it was enhanced reliance on automatic ideation or instead a lack of controlled processing that related to lower quality judgments in those exhibiting higher JTC behavior. Using belief bias and denominator neglect, we assessed how much participants gave weight to automatic versus controlled processes in their decision making.

Using Jacoby's (1991) process dissociation scheme, we took questions from the belief bias tests and the denominator neglect task and parsed out whether they associated with automatic or controlled processes.

[PAPER_0101, relevance_score=0.261] To assess JTC, we summed the number of fish they asked to see across the two lakes, with the number they requested quite highly correlated across the two lakes, r(287) = .81, p < .001, in Study 1a and r(296) = .79, p < .001, in Study 1b. To reduce potential skew and kurtosis, we took the natural log of this sum.

[PAPER_0102, relevance_score=0.329] To reduce potential skew and kurtosis, we took the natural log of this sum. Then we reverse coded this number by subtracting the natural log of the maximum amount of fish that could be viewed by the natural log of the number of fish viewed (2.772589 - the natural log of the sum of the fish). For example, if a participant viewed two fish from the first lake and three fish from the second, JTC was calculated in the following manner (2 + 3 = 5; ln(5) = 1.609).

[PAPER_0103, relevance_score=0.281] Then we reverse coded by taking the calculated number and subtracting the natural log of the maximum number of fish that could have been viewed across both lakes which was 16 (ln(16) = 2.772589). Reverse coding ensures those that collected less information are classified as higher on JTC. In our example, the jumping score would be 2.772589 - 1.609 = 1.164.

[PAPER_0181, relevance_score=0.287] For example, after standardizing scores on system 1 bias measures (i.e., belief bias, CRT performance, and denominator neglect) so that they shared a common scale, a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) showed that JTC was significantly and positively correlated with their expression, F(1, 287) = 34.68, p < .001, ηp2 = .36 in Study 1a and F(1, 296) = 69.84, p < .001, ηp2 = .44, in Study 1b.
